titleText.es: Hace poco uno me dijo que buscara un ordenador y lo encendiera para poder reiniciarlo. Se negaba a avanzar en su guión antes de que le dijera que había hecho eso.
titleText.en: I recently had someone ask me to go get a computer and turn it on so I could restart it. He refused to move further in the script until I said I had done that.
titleText.noteEn: These are the exact title texts from the Spanish archive and official xkcd metadata. The archive preserves the spelling guión used by the translator.

regions.labelEs: ¿REINICIAR MI ORDENADOR? YA SÉ QUE DEBE SEGUIR UN GUIÓN, PERO LA LUZ UPLINK DEL MÓDEM SE APAGA CADA POCAS HORAS. EL PROBLEMA ESTÁ ENTRE SU OFICINA Y EL MÓDEM.

applications.explanationEn: Debe changes for the formal listener, while seguir stays in its unchanged -ir dictionary form.
Debe has the same singular form used with él or ella, but here it addresses one listener formally.
Cada marks recurrence, pocas matches the feminine plural horas, and the full expression gives an inexact interval.
Problema is masculine despite ending in -a, so it takes the masculine article el.

applications.exampleEs: ENTRE SU OFICINA Y EL MÓDEM
applications.explanationEn: Entre introduces the first endpoint, and y introduces the second endpoint of the stated location.

applications.exampleEs: ESTÁ ENTRE SU OFICINA Y EL MÓDEM
applications.explanationEn: Está is a form of estar because the phrase beginning with entre locates the problem rather than identifying what it is.

regions.labelEs: MI ORDENADOR NO TIENE NADA QUE VER... VALE, DA IGUAL, HE "REINICIADO MI ORDENADOR".

applications.explanationEn: No and nada reinforce the denial, while tener que ver forms the fixed expression about having a connection or relevance.
Da igual is the fixed conversational expression used to dismiss the distinction.
He is the present form of haber for the speaker, and reiniciado is the unchanged completed-action form used after it.

regions.labelEs: SIGUE CAÍDO, Y AUNQUE VOLVIESE, VOLVERÍA A CAERSE DENTRO DE UNAS HORAS, PORQUE SU...

applications.explanationEn: Sigue says that the condition continues, and caído names the continuing down or offline state.
Aunque introduces the imagined condition, and volviese is the -se form of volver used for that unreal possibility.
The -ría ending makes volvería the conditional form used for the imagined result.
Volvería changes for the imagined situation, a links it to the repeated action, and caerse stays in its dictionary form.
Dentro de introduces a period measured forward from the current reference point, and unas horas gives its approximate length.

regions.labelEs: NO TENGO MENÚ INICIO. ESTO ES UN SISTEMA HAIKU, PERO NO ES RELEVAN...

applications.explanationEn: Es is a form of ser because the noun phrase un sistema Haiku identifies what esto is rather than locating it.

regions.labelEs: ¿HAIKU? ES UN SISTEMA OPERATIVO EXPERIMENTAL QUE HE... EH, DA IGUAL.

applications.explanationEn: Es is a form of ser because the following noun phrase classifies what Haiku is rather than stating a location.
Sistema is masculine despite ending in -a, so un and the -o form operativo match it.
Sistema and operativo form the conventional Spanish term for an operating system.
The noun sistema comes first, followed by operativo and experimental as descriptions.
Operativo uses masculine singular -o to match sistema; experimental is singular and has the same gender-neutral form here.
Da igual closes the abandoned explanation with the fixed expression meaning that the topic no longer matters.

regions.labelEs: LO SIENTO, PERO ESTO NUNCA SE ARREGLARÁ HASTA QUE HABLE CON UN INGENIERO. ¿VE CERCA DE USTED A ALGUIEN QUE LLEVE PANTALONES CARGO, QUIZÁS CON UN MAPA DEL METRO PEGADO EN LA PARED?

applications.explanationEn: Lo siento is the conventional two-word apology.
Se leaves the person doing the repair unnamed, while arreglará states the future repair event.
The ending -ará places the repair after the present time.
Hasta que introduces a conversation that has not happened yet, so hablar appears as hable.
Ve has the singular third-person shape but politely addresses the listener as usted.
Question marks and intonation turn the ordinary verb form ve into a yes-or-no question without adding a Spanish equivalent of English “do.”
Cerca requires de before the nearby person, and usted names that person formally.
Usted explicitly marks formal singular “you” and takes singular third-person verb forms.
A appears before alguien because the unknown person directly receives the action of seeing.
Alguien leaves the person unidentified, and lleve uses the special form for a characteristic the speaker is seeking.

regions.labelEs: HAY UNA TÍA DOS MESAS MÁS ALLÁ CON UN PINGÜINO DE PELUCHE Y UN PÓSTER DE UN TIPO CON BARBA CON ESPADAS.

applications.explanationEn: Más and allá combine into the fixed adverbial expression for a farther or more distant position.
Here de identifies the toy's plush material.

regions.labelEs: PERFECTO, ¿PUEDE PASÁRMELA?

applications.explanationEn: Puede uses the singular form associated with usted, making the request formal without repeating usted.
Puede changes for the formal listener, while pasar remains in its unchanged -ar form inside pasármela.
Me and la attach to the unchanged verb pasar; me marks the caller as receiver and la refers to the woman being transferred.
The ordinary sequence puede pasármela becomes a polite yes-or-no question through question marks and intonation.

regions.labelEs: CLARO.
HOLA, PERDONE QUE LA MOLESTE, PERO MI CONEXIÓN...

applications.explanationEn: Perdone is perdonar's usted command and works here as the polite formula “excuse me.”
Perdone opens the formal apology, que introduces the interruption, la marks the formal listener as the person affected, and moleste takes the form used after this apology.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, YA VEO. ES UN PROBLEMA RECURRENTE POR UN CAMBIO DE SERVIDOR.

applications.explanationEn: Es uses ser because the noun phrase classifies the issue rather than locating it.
Problema is masculine despite ending in -a, so it takes un.
The noun problema comes first and the description recurrente follows it.
Recurrente is singular to match problema and has the same form with masculine and feminine nouns.

regions.labelEs: TECLEA
YA DEBERÍA IR BIEN.

applications.explanationEn: Debería expresses an expectation here, and ir remains in its unchanged form as the expected action.
Ir describes how the system functions, not movement to a place.

regions.labelEs: MUCHÍSIMAS GRACIAS.

applications.explanationEn: The ending -ísimas intensifies muchas and also keeps the feminine plural agreement used in this conventional thanks expression.

regions.labelEs: SIN PROBLEMA. MIRE, EN EL FUTURO, DURANTE UNA LLAMADA AL SERVICIO TÉCNICO, PUEDE DECIR LA PALABRA "SHIBBOLEET" EN CUALQUIER MOMENTO Y AUTOMÁTICAMENTE SE LE PASARÁ CON UNA PERSONA QUE CONOZCA COMO MÍNIMO DOS LENGUAJES DE PROGRAMACIÓN.

applications.explanationEn: Sin problema is the conventional compact reassurance that something causes no difficulty.
Mire is mirar's usted command, used politely to direct one listener's attention.
Servicio técnico is the conventional term for a technical support or repair service.
Servicio names the service first, and técnico follows as its description.
Técnico uses masculine singular -o to match servicio.
Puede changes for the formal listener, while decir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Puede uses the singular form associated with usted while referring to the formal listener.
En introduces a time point, and cualquier momento leaves that point unrestricted.
Cualquier appears before the singular noun momento; Spanish does not use cualquiera before a following noun.
The -mente ending turns automática into an adverb describing how the transfer happens.
Se leaves the support worker performing the transfer unnamed, le identifies the recipient, and pasará states the future action.
The ending -ará places the transfer after the present time.
Le identifies the caller being transferred, pasará supplies the transfer action, and con introduces the person reached on the other end.
Persona is not an identified individual, so the description after que uses conozca for the required but not-yet-known person.
Como mínimo is the fixed expression that sets a lower numerical threshold.
Lenguajes takes the plural form, and de programación identifies the field those languages belong to.

regions.labelEs: ¿EN SERIO?

applications.explanationEn: En serio is the fixed expression used here as a short question asking whether the claim is genuine.

regions.labelEs: SÍ. ES UNA PUERTA TRASERA QUE PUSIERON LOS GEEKS QUE MONTARON ESTOS SISTEMAS DE SOPORTE TELEFÓNICO EN LOS 90. NO SE LO DIGA A NADIE.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed decade numeral is a number, not a Spanish lexical word target.

applications.explanationEn: Es uses ser because una puerta trasera identifies what the hidden mechanism is rather than where it is.
Puerta names the thing first, and trasera follows as its description.
Trasera uses feminine singular -a to match puerta.
Puerta trasera is the thing described, que connects it to the added information, and pusieron supplies the completed action.
Pusieron presents the installation as a completed event in the past.
Geeks is the group described, que links it to the description, and montaron supplies the completed action.
Montaron presents the setup as a completed past event.
Soporte names the service first, and telefónico follows as its description.
Telefónico uses masculine singular -o to match soporte.
Se replaces le before the direct-object pronoun lo; the two short pronouns keep recipient first and thing said second.
Diga is decir's irregular usted command; no before it makes the instruction negative.

applications.exampleEs: NO SE LO DIGA A NADIE
applications.explanationEn: No appears before the command verb, while nadie follows it; Spanish keeps both negative elements in this order.

regions.labelEs: DIOS MÍO, ESTO ES LO MEJ...

applications.explanationEn: Dios mío is the conventional exclamation, with mío following the noun.
Es uses ser because the interrupted nominal phrase beginning with lo identifies how the speaker classifies esto.
Lo turns the cut-off describing word mej… into the start of the fixed nominal expression lo mejor.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks a question.

regions.labelEs: ...MIERDA.

cards.answerEn: already; by now, often yet in a question
cards.noteEn: Ya marks that an expected action or state has been reached by the time being discussed. English usually says 'already' in a statement, but often 'yet' in a question about whether it has happened.

cards.answerEn: that; links an expression to its content or an outcome
cards.noteEn: Que can introduce what someone thinks, says, wants, causes, or allows, or what an evaluation is about. English may use 'that,' omit it, or reorganize the sentence with 'to' or 'for.' Que stays unaccented; the following verb form depends on the surrounding expression.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.

cards.answerEn: Use the same singular verb form used with él or ella (“he” or “she”).
cards.noteEn: Although usted refers to the listener, Spanish treats it like “he” or “she” when choosing the verb. Compare tú necesitas for informal “you need” with usted necesita for formal “you need.” Spanish often leaves usted unspoken when the context makes it clear.
cards.questionEn: When usted means polite or formal “you,” which verb form goes with it?

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; presents something as undergoing a change
cards.noteEn: With some verbs, se makes the named thing the one that changes, rather than the thing someone changes. Compare Marta abre la puerta with la puerta se abre. The verb still changes for the thing and time; se does not say that it deliberately acts on itself.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens every few days, weeks, months, or similar periods?
cards.answerEn: Use cada, then pocos or pocas, then the plural time period.
cards.noteEn: Pocos or pocas matches the time noun: cada pocos días, cada pocas semanas, cada pocos meses. This describes a recurring interval without saying its exact length.

cards.promptEs: el/un problema y otros sustantivos masculinos en -ma
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish say un problema even though problema ends in -a?
cards.answerEn: Problema is masculine, so use el or un and masculine describing words with it.
cards.noteEn: A noun's ending is only a clue to its gender, not an absolute rule. Several common words of Greek origin ending in -ma are masculine, including el problema, el sistema, el tema, and el programa. Learn each noun together with its article because not every word ending in -ma follows this pattern.

Está is a form of estar for he, she, it, or one person addressed formally as usted. It describes where someone or something is, or their condition. The surrounding words identify the person; Spanish need not add a separate word for he, she, it, or formal you.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.promptEs: entre + elemento A + y + elemento B
cards.questionEn: How do you frame two endpoints or sides as a range, pair, or contrast?
cards.answerEn: Place entre before the first endpoint or side and y before the second one.
cards.noteEn: Entre marks the range or pair involved, and y joins its two sides. Each side may be a single word or a longer noun group.

example.es: No veo la diferencia entre el azul oscuro y el negro.
example.en: I do not see the difference between dark blue and black.

cards.answerEn: his; her; its; their; your, with usted or ustedes
cards.noteEn: Su comes before one possessed thing. It does not show the owner's gender or number: context tells you whose it is. Use sus when the possessed things are plural, even if there is only one owner: su libro, but sus libros. Formal usted and plural ustedes also use su for 'your.'

example.es: Ana abre su libro; los niños abren su caja.
example.en: Ana opens her book; the children open their box.

cards.promptEs: no tener nada que ver con…
cards.answerEn: Use no with a form of tener, then nada que ver. Add con before the unrelated person, thing, or topic.
cards.noteEn: This is a fixed expression; ver does not mean literally “to see” here. Use con to name the unrelated subject. You can leave that subject unsaid when the conversation already makes it clear.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing has no connection to another?

example.es: Eso no tiene nada que ver con el precio.
example.en: That has nothing to do with the price.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word (part of nada que ver)
connection; relevance (inside nada que ver con)
cards.noteEn: Ver normally means “to see.” Inside no tener nada que ver con, however, it is part of a fixed expression about having no connection or involvement; translating ver alone as “see” would be misleading.

example.es: Eso no tiene nada que ver con el precio.
example.en: That has nothing to do with the price.

cards.answerEn: doesn't matter (as part of da igual)
Da igual means “it doesn't matter” or “either way is fine.”
cards.noteEn: Treat da igual as a fixed expression rather than translating its two words separately. Add me, te, or le to say who does not mind: me da igual means “I don't mind.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that a choice or difference does not matter?

example.es: Da igual; las dos opciones son buenas.
example.en: It doesn't matter; both options are good.

cards.answerEn: doesn't matter (as part of da igual)
Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.answerEn: Use a form of seguir followed by the word that describes the condition.
cards.noteEn: Seguir normally means “to continue” or “to keep going.” Before a description, it means “to still be” or “to remain”: sigue abierta means “is still open.” If the describing word has masculine, feminine, singular, or plural endings, match it to what is being described.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is still in the same condition?

cards.promptEs: aunque seguido de una situación imaginada en -ra o -se
cards.questionEn: How do you use aunque to say 'even if' about an imagined or unlikely situation?
cards.answerEn: Use aunque and a special verb form such as tuviera or tuviese for the imagined condition.
cards.noteEn: These forms are called the imperfect subjunctive. Here they present a possibility as imagined or remote, not necessarily as an event in the past. An ordinary tiene ('has') becomes tuviera or tuviese ('had' in 'even if she had'); llueve becomes lloviera or lloviese. The main part often uses a would-form such as iría, 'would go.' Aunque can also introduce known facts, but that is a different use.

example.en: Even if it rained, we would go.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of volver, then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form of a verb is called the infinitive. It usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as hablar, comer, or salir. Only volver changes to show who acts and when; the final verb stays in its dictionary form. In this pattern, volver a means repeating the action, not literally returning to a place.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something again?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; it links volver to the repeated action
to go down; to become unavailable (a service or system)
cards.noteEn: Caerse can describe a website, service, or system stopping working. It is not a physical fall in this use. The attached se belongs to this verb use; a changed form is el servicio se cae, “the service goes down.”

example.es: La web puede caerse si hay demasiadas visitas.
example.en: The website can go down if it gets too many visits.

cards.noteEn: Dentro de followed by a length of time looks forward from now: dentro de una semana means “in a week.”

example.en: I will return in an hour.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something will happen a certain amount of time from now?
cards.answerEn: Use dentro de before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Dentro de looks forward from the present: dentro de dos horas means “in two hours.” This differs from hace dos horas, which looks backward and means “two hours ago.”

example.es: El tren sale dentro de media hora.
example.en: The train leaves in half an hour.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes dentro de, “in”
cards.noteEn: When dentro de introduces a future delay, translate the two words together as “in.”

example.es: La película empieza dentro de diez minutos.
example.en: The movie starts in ten minutes.

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

Es is a present form of ser for one person or thing, including usted, the formal way to address one person as 'you.' It can identify, classify, describe, evaluate, or state a time. Spanish can leave the person or thing understood, where English supplies 'he,' 'she,' or 'it.' Compare es with eres for familiar 'you' and son for several people or things.
The unusual operating system derails the scripted support conversation.
cards.questionEn: What is Haiku in a computer-support conversation?
How do you say “operating system” in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Say sistema operativo; use sistemas operativos for more than one.
cards.noteEn: This is the conventional computing term. Sistema is masculine despite ending in -a, so operativo uses the masculine form and both words become plural together.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: A hesitation sound used while the speaker pauses to think or find words. This is different from eh used to call for attention or ask for agreement.

cards.answerEn: it (in the fixed apology lo siento, I'm sorry)

cards.questionEn: How do you say 'I'm sorry' or 'we're sorry' with lo siento?
cards.answerEn: Use lo siento when speaking for yourself and lo sentimos when speaking for a group.
cards.noteEn: Use this conventional expression for an apology or for sympathy about bad news. Lo stays fixed, while sentir changes to siento for I and sentimos for we. Mucho can strengthen the apology: lo siento mucho. These are variations of the same expression, not separate meanings of apology.

example.en: We're sorry. It was a mistake.

cards.answerEn: I feel (in lo siento: I'm sorry)
no separate English word; focuses on what receives an action, without naming the doer
cards.noteEn: Se can present the thing acted on without naming who acts. The verb normally matches that thing: se vende una casa, but se venden dos casas. English often uses 'is' or 'are' plus a form such as 'sold.' Adding poder expresses possibility without changing se's role.

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona (sin nombrar quién actúa)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish focus on an action or result without naming who does it?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person verb and state what happens; the person doing it can remain unnamed.
cards.noteEn: English often uses a passive form. Spanish may use se with a simple verb or with a completed construction such as se han encontrado. Other uses of se follow different patterns.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: adding -á to sentir gives sentirá, and adding -á to ver gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.answerEn: Use the subjunctive for the still-awaited action.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special Spanish verb form used here because the action is still pending. In esperaré hasta que llegues, the arrival has not happened yet. After the event has already happened, Spanish uses its ordinary statement form instead: esperé hasta que llegaste means “I waited until you arrived.”
cards.questionEn: After hasta que (“until”), which verb form do you use for something that has not happened yet?

example.en: I will wait until you arrive.

cards.noteEn: Con introduces someone or something accompanying, involved in, or used for an action. It does not change for the person or time. Some verbs require it, as in hablar con alguien, 'to talk with someone.'

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.promptEs: cerca de + persona, lugar o cosa
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is near a person, place, or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use cerca de, followed by the nearby person, place, or thing.
cards.noteEn: Cerca is followed by de in this pattern. When el follows, de and el combine as del: cerca del parque.
Cerca normally uses de before the nearby person, place, or thing.

example.es: La estación está cerca de casa.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person or animate target directly acted on
cards.noteEn: Spanish usually puts a before a known person directly affected by a verb, and before person words such as alguien or nadie. Animals and things treated as person-like can also take it. This does not mean movement 'to' someone or giving something to a recipient.

example.es: Veo a Marta, pero no veo a su perro.
example.en: I see Marta, but I do not see her dog.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. When a comes directly before the masculine article el, combine the two words as al.

cards.promptEs: persona o cosa no identificada + que + descripción
cards.questionEn: How do you choose the verb after que when describing someone or something that has not been identified?
cards.answerEn: Use the special subjunctive form when you want any suitable person or thing, or are not treating its existence as established.
cards.noteEn: Name the person or thing, add que ('who' or 'that'), then describe it. Subjunctive is the name for verb forms used here for a wanted or possible description rather than a known example. Compare conozco a alguien que habla inglés, 'I know someone who speaks English,' with busco a alguien que hable inglés, 'I am looking for someone who speaks English.' Habla changes to hable because no particular suitable person is identified. Similar choices occur after cualquier ('any') or when a suitable thing may not exist; the word que alone does not force this form.

example.es: Necesito un libro que explique esto.
example.en: I need a book that explains this.

cards.noteEn: Hay introduces what exists, is present, or is available. It stays unchanged for one thing or several: hay una tienda, hay dos tiendas. English changes 'there is' to 'there are,' but Spanish does not change hay. The English 'there' in this pattern does not point to a place. Inside a description such as la tienda que hay aquí, English can instead say 'the shop that is here'; Spanish hay still introduces what is present.

cards.answerEn: farther (as part of más allá, farther away)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is farther away or beyond a point?
cards.answerEn: Use más allá; add de before a named reference point.
cards.noteEn: Más allá works as a fixed place expression. It can stand alone for “farther away,” or appear as más allá de followed by the place, limit, or idea that is exceeded.

example.es: El pueblo está más allá de la colina.
example.en: The town is beyond the hill.

cards.answerEn: of; made of or from (introducing a material)
cards.noteEn: After an object or an expression such as ser de or estar hecho de, de introduces the material that composes it.

example.en: The door is made of metal.

cards.noteEn: In informal speech, tipo can refer to a man as “guy.” In other contexts, it can instead mean a type or kind.

cards.answerEn: can you; could you (formal or polite request)
cards.noteEn: In a question to one person addressed formally as usted, puede followed by an action can make a polite request. Puede has the same written form used for he, she, or it.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: to pass her to me; put her on
cards.noteEn: Pasármela combines pasar with me and la: pasar means “to pass,” me means “to me,” and la replaces a feminine person or thing. These small words attach to the verb's unchanged dictionary form, creating one written word.

example.en: The bottle is over there; can you pass it to me?

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Small words naming who or what receives the action can attach directly: conocer and te become conocerte, and ayudar and me become ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: Use the usted command form: regular -ar verbs end in -e, while regular -er and -ir verbs end in -a.
cards.noteEn: Usted is the polite or formal singular “you.” Hablar becomes hable, comer becomes coma, and escribir becomes escriba. Usted is usually left out because the command ending already shows formal address. Some common verbs are irregular, such as decir becoming diga.
cards.questionEn: How do you politely tell one person to do something in Spanish?

cards.answerEn: Say perdone que, followed by the action you are apologizing for. It works like “excuse me for” or “sorry to.”
cards.noteEn: Perdone is the polite form used when addressing one person formally. The verb after que uses a special form called the subjunctive because the speaker is apologizing for the action rather than simply reporting it. With someone you address informally, use perdona que instead.
cards.questionEn: How can you formally apologize before interrupting or bothering someone?

cards.answerEn: her; it; formal you, for one woman
cards.noteEn: La can replace a woman or a thing whose Spanish name is feminine when it directly receives an action. It can also address one woman formally as usted. It usually comes before a changed verb; it does not mean the article 'the' in this use.

example.es: Tengo una carta y la leo.
example.en: I have a letter and I am reading it.

cards.noteEn: Por can introduce the cause or reason for something, before a noun or an action in its dictionary form. It explains why something happens, not the goal someone wants to achieve.

example.es: Cerraron la calle por la nieve.
example.en: They closed the street because of the snow.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to its type, purpose, or field
cards.noteEn: Spanish often puts de between two nouns where English puts the describing noun first. In una silla de oficina, oficina tells you the chair's intended use. This is different from de naming an owner, material, contents, or a part's larger whole.
Teclea is a present form of teclear used for one person or thing, or for formal singular “you.” As a brief action label, it reports that one person is typing.

cards.answerEn: It can say that something is expected or likely to happen.
cards.noteEn: Context decides between advice and expectation. Deberías descansar tells a person what they should do. El tren debería llegar pronto predicts what is expected to happen. In both uses, the following action stays in its dictionary form.
cards.questionEn: Besides giving advice, what can debería followed by a verb mean?

cards.answerEn: to work; to run; to function
cards.noteEn: Ir can describe how a system, machine, or process works rather than movement to a place. A following description says how it is running: ir bien, “to work well,” or ir lento, “to run slowly.”

example.es: El ordenador debería ir más rápido.

cards.questionEn: How can you intensify a Spanish description or quantity to mean “very” or “extremely”?
cards.answerEn: Replace the word's usual ending with the matching form -ísimo, -ísima, -ísimos, or -ísimas.
cards.noteEn: The ending matches the gender and number of what is described. For example, mucho becomes muchísimo, muchísima, muchísimos, or muchísimas. Some bases also change spelling or written stress, so common forms should be learned with their accents.

cards.questionEn: How can you reassure someone with “no problem”?
cards.noteEn: This conventional reply combines sin, “without,” with problema. The plural sin problemas can instead describe doing something without difficulties.
Al combines a and el into one word. Spanish requires this combined form when the two occur together.

cards.questionEn: How do you name a technical support or repair service?
cards.noteEn: This conventional term can refer to technical support or to a service that diagnoses and repairs products. Técnico follows servicio and matches its masculine singular form.

cards.questionEn: Where does the invented word shibboleet come from?
cards.answerEn: It blends shibboleth, a signal of belonging to a group, with leet, internet slang associated with technical insiders.
cards.noteEn: A shibboleth can be a word, pronunciation, or custom that distinguishes insiders from outsiders. Leet comes from 'elite' and is often written 1337 using digit substitutions. Their blend suggests an insider's identifying code.
Before a specific moment, en can correspond to English “at.”

example.en: He arrived at just the right moment.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something may happen at any time?
cards.noteEn: En introduces a point in time, and cualquier before the singular noun momento leaves that point unrestricted.

example.en: You can call at any time.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “any” before one singular thing?
cards.answerEn: Put cualquier before a singular noun: cualquier libro, cualquier opción.
cards.noteEn: A noun is a naming word such as libro or opción. Before a noun, cualquiera shortens to cualquier. The noun stays singular even when the meaning is any one out of many.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.
This se presents the action without naming who performs it. A following le can identify the person who receives or is affected by the action.

example.en: A message will be sent to you.

cards.noteEn: When addressing someone formally, le can mean “to you.” It is an indirect-object pronoun and normally appears before the conjugated verb.

example.en: I’ll write to you tomorrow, sir.

cards.promptEs: pasar a alguien con otra persona (por teléfono)
cards.questionEn: How do you say that a caller is put through to another person or department?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of pasar for the transfer, then con before the person or department reached.
cards.noteEn: Pasar changes for the person and time. The caller may appear as a short pronoun, as in me pasaron con ventas, while con introduces the destination of the telephone transfer.

example.en: Can you put me through to sales?

cards.answerEn: will be passed; will be transferred
to; with (introducing the destination of a phone transfer)
cards.noteEn: After pasar in a telephone context, con introduces the person or department that the caller is put through to.

example.en: They put me through to reception.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins como mínimo, “at least”
cards.noteEn: Como often means “as” or “like,” but in the fixed expression como mínimo it helps set a lower limit.

example.en: We need at least three chairs.

cards.answerEn: Como mínimo means “at least” or “at a minimum.”
cards.noteEn: Place this expression next to the relevant amount. Here como belongs to the whole expression and does not mean “like.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that a number is the lowest possible or required amount?

example.en: We need at least three people.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “programming language”?
cards.answerEn: Say lenguaje de programación; use lenguajes de programación for more than one.
cards.noteEn: De programación identifies the field or purpose of the language. Only lenguaje changes to mark the plural.

example.es: Python es un lenguaje de programación.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en serio (“seriously”)

cards.questionEn: How do you ask whether someone is really serious or whether something is actually true?
cards.answerEn: Use en serio to mean “seriously,” “really,” or “for real.”
cards.noteEn: En serio is a fixed expression. In a question, ¿En serio? often reacts with surprise or disbelief; in a statement, it can contrast sincerity with joking.

example.en: Are you really going to run tomorrow?

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.answerEn: a hidden access path that bypasses normal controls
cards.noteEn: A backdoor bypasses the normal route or controls; the term can be used literally in technology or metaphorically for a hidden shortcut.
cards.questionEn: What is a backdoor in a computer system?

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.answerEn: to them/anyone; replaces le before lo
cards.noteEn: When le or les comes immediately before lo, la, los, or las, it changes to se. This se identifies the recipient; it is not reflexive.

example.es: Le doy el libro a Ana. → Se lo doy.
example.en: I give the book to Ana. → I give it to her.

cards.promptEs: le/les + lo/la/los/las → se lo/se la/se los/se las
cards.answerEn: Use se for the recipient, followed by lo, la, los, or las for the thing.
cards.noteEn: Le or les normally means “to him,” “to her,” “to you” (formal), or “to them.” Immediately before lo, la, los, or las, it changes to se; Spanish does not say le lo. Se still stands for the recipient, while the second word stands for the thing. Le doy el libro a Ana therefore becomes se lo doy.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “I give it to her/him/them” without repeating the person and the thing?

example.es: Le doy el libro a Ana. → Se lo doy.
example.en: I give the book to Ana. → I give it to her.

cards.answerEn: it; that, as the thing or idea acted on
cards.noteEn: Lo can replace a masculine singular thing or a whole idea that receives an action. It usually comes before the verb and does not name who performs the action. English often uses 'it' or 'that'; with todo, lo can refer to everything being acted on.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I am reading it.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nadie is commonly translated as “anyone.” Spanish uses negative concord, so no and nadie can appear together.

cards.questionEn: How do you exclaim “my God”?
cards.noteEn: Dios mío can express shock, frustration, or a literal address to God. Mío follows Dios and agrees with its masculine form.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you use lo to mean 'the good part,' 'what is important,' or another general quality?
cards.answerEn: Put lo before the masculine singular form of a describing word, without adding a noun.
cards.noteEn: A describing word is called an adjective: bueno means good and difícil means difficult. Lo turns that quality into a general thing or aspect, as in lo bueno ('the good part') and lo difícil ('what is difficult'). It does not refer to a masculine object. Keep the describing word masculine singular: lo bueno, not lo buena or lo buenos. Lo mejor likewise means the best thing or part; mejor itself supplies 'best.'

Qué means “what” in ¿Qué quieres? (“What do you want?”) and “which” in ¿Qué libro quieres? (“Which book do you want?”). You can also use it to say what you do not know: No sé qué elegir means “I do not know what to choose.”

example.en: I do not know which route to choose.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
